catalog_quote: Stress is not phonologically distinctive in Awa Pit. There are no words which are distinguished by stress, and while speakers seem to have a preferred stress for each word, for some words different speakers stress the word differently (in isolation); sometimes the same speaker will stress the word differently on different occasions. The morphology and syntax also interact with the stress: words normally stressed on one syllable may be stressed on a different syllable depending on the morphemes or words surrounding it. It should be noted that while the stress may shift, each phonological word does receive a stress somewhere, at least in slow speech. As stress is not distinctive (and indeed my informants would never correct me if I repeated a word after them with a different stress pattern), it will not be dealt with here any further. new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the modern reference grammar (Curnow 1997): every phonological word bears one main stress, but its position is not contrastive and not fixed - it varies across speakers, across repetitions by the same speaker, and with the surrounding morphemes/words; the author declines to state any placement rule. The older SIL phonology (Henriksen & Henriksen 1979:60) instead calls stress lexically contrastive at word level (/pímpul/ vs /pankúl/, /akwán/ vs /ákwa/), and its orthography (p.62) writes the accent only 'cuando no está en la sílaba penúltima', i.e. treats penultimate as the unmarked position. The two primary sources therefore disagree (non-contrastive/variable vs lexical with penult default); no source states a fixed weight-blind rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Curnow: stress shifts depending on adjacent clitics/morphemes and words; possible extraprosodic morphology flagged but not analysed; informants never corrected mis-stressed repetitions. Henriksen & Henriksen 1979:60: the pause-group (phrase-final) accent is more intense and higher-pitched than lexical accents.
new_statements.domain_note: Curnow's remarks concern the phonological word, both citation forms ('in isolation') and connected speech ('at least in slow speech'); Henriksen & Henriksen distinguish word-level lexical accent from a pause-marking (phrase) accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Curnow 1997 describes Colombian Awa Pit (fieldwork mainly around Pialapí/Pueblo Viejo, Nariño); Henriksen & Henriksen 1979 describe 'Cuaiquer' of the Ricaurte-Altaquer area, Nariño, Colombia - same language (awac1239, ISO kwi), Colombian side. The Ecuadorian variety (Montaluisa 1992) was not seen. Note the Rosetta Project/Internet Archive items are misfiled under code 'awb' (a PNG language) but their content and printed citations are unambiguously Henriksen & Henriksen 1979 on Colombian Cuaiquer.

sources.note: Section 2.5.2 'Stress', p.46 (PDF p.67): stress is not phonologically distinctive; no words distinguished by stress; speakers have a preferred stress per word but placement varies between and within speakers and shifts with surrounding morphemes/words; every phonological word receives a stress somewhere in slow speech; no placement rule given, explicitly left for future work (clitics, extraprosodic morphology). p.82: 'Each phonological word carries a main stress'. No other stress/accent statements in the thesis (searched full text).
